issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary inquiry against a public employee cannot be discontinued merely because a criminal investigation into the same allegations does not warrant criminal action.
material_facts: Disciplinary charges were issued against a public employee concerning alleged irregularities in the allotment and conversion of plots.
The disciplinary inquiry was kept in abeyance while the CBI investigated overlapping allegations.
After receiving the CBI report, the State discontinued the disciplinary inquiry on the ground that the report did not warrant action on the same points.
The stated basis for discontinuing the inquiry did not account for the different purposes and standards of proof in disciplinary and criminal proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The decision to discontinue the disciplinary inquiry was unreasonable and untenable, was quashed, and the inquiry was directed to continue.
issues.legal_principle: Executive decisions must satisfy the standard of reasonableness (Tata Cellular v. Union of India; Teri Oat Estates (P.) Ltd. v. U.T. Chandigarh). Disciplinary proceedings maintain service discipline and assess misconduct under applicable service rules, whereas criminal proceedings determine criminal liability under the criminal standard of proof and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the Evidence Act's strict rules of proof do not govern disciplinary inquiries. An acquittal or a criminal investigation's outcome does not automatically bar disciplinary action. The Court relied on Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan v. T. Srinivas, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Sarvesh Berry, Uttaranchal Road Transport Corporation v. Mansaram Nainwal, Depot Manager, A.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Mohd. Yousuf Miya, State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena, Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., and Union of India v. Bihari Lal Sidhana.

predicates.disciplinary_inquiry_against_public_empl: A disciplinary inquiry was initiated against a public employee concerning alleged misconduct.
predicates.inquiry_discontinued_after_criminal_inve: The disciplinary inquiry was discontinued after a criminal investigation into the allegations had taken place.
predicates.discontinuance_based_on_criminal_report_: The authority relied on the criminal investigation's report alone as the basis for discontinuing the disciplinary inquiry.

issues.definition: When a disciplinary inquiry against a public employee is discontinued after a criminal investigation solely because of that investigation's report, the discontinuance is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary inquiry may generally proceed alongside a criminal trial, but a stay may be appropriate where the criminal charge is grave and complex and the disciplinary inquiry would seriously prejudice the employee's defence.
material_facts: The disciplinary inquiry and criminal investigation concerned overlapping allegations against the employee.
The disciplinary inquiry had been stayed while the CBI investigation was pending and was later discontinued.
The employee indicated that a request could be made to keep the disciplinary inquiry in abeyance pending the criminal proceedings.
The Court directed that any such request be considered under the principles governing parallel disciplinary and criminal proceedings, including the risk of prejudice and undue delay.
issues.conclusion: There is no inflexible rule requiring a disciplinary inquiry to be stayed during a criminal case. Any request for a stay must be considered on the case's facts, including whether the criminal charge is grave, whether it involves complicated questions of fact and law, whether the inquiry would seriously prejudice the defence, and whether the proceedings are being unduly delayed.
issues.legal_principle: Departmental and criminal proceedings may ordinarily proceed simultaneously. It is desirable to stay the departmental proceedings when they rest on identical or similar facts and the criminal charge is grave and involves complicated questions of fact and law, but those factors must be considered alongside prejudice to the employee's defence and the risk of undue delay. A stay is not an inflexible rule, and disciplinary proceedings may be resumed if the criminal case does not proceed or its disposal is unduly delayed. The Court relied on Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., Depot Manager, A.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Mohd. Yousuf Miya, State of Rajasthan v. B.K. Meena, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. v. Sarvesh Berry, and Uttaranchal Road Transport Corporation v. Mansaram Nainwal.

rule.if: simultaneous_disciplinary_and_criminal_proceedings and identical_or_similar_facts and grave_criminal_charge and complicated_criminal_questions and serious_prejudice_to_defence and not undue_delay_in_disciplinary_proceedings

predicates.simultaneous_disciplinary_and_criminal_p: A disciplinary inquiry and a criminal trial are pending against the same employee at the same time.
predicates.identical_or_similar_facts: The disciplinary inquiry and criminal trial concern identical or substantially similar facts.
predicates.grave_criminal_charge: The criminal charge against the employee is grave in nature.
predicates.complicated_criminal_questions: The criminal case involves complicated questions of fact or law.
predicates.serious_prejudice_to_defence: Continuing the disciplinary inquiry would seriously prejudice the employee's defence in the criminal trial.
predicates.undue_delay_in_disciplinary_proceedings: The disciplinary proceedings are being unduly delayed.

issues.definition: Where parallel proceedings concern similar facts, the criminal charge is grave and complex, the disciplinary inquiry would seriously prejudice the defence, and the disciplinary proceedings are not unduly delayed, a stay of the disciplinary proceedings is desirable.
